hints: Write $\cot x=\cos x/\sin x$ and apply the quotient rule.
The numerator becomes $-\sin^2x-\cos^2x$; use the Pythagorean identity and divide by $\sin^2x$.
walkthrough:
Apply the quotient rule $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$ to $y = \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$ with $u = \cos x$ and $v = \sin x$:
$$u' = -\sin x, \quad v' = \cos x$$

Form the derivative expression:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{(-\sin x)(\sin x) - (\cos x)(\cos x)}{\sin^2 x} = \dfrac{-\sin^2 x - \cos^2 x}{\sin^2 x}$$

Factor $-1$ in the numerator and apply the identity $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{-(\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x)}{\sin^2 x} = \dfrac{-1}{\sin^2 x} = -\operatorname{cosec}^2 x$$
This completes the proof.

hints: Use integration by parts with $u=x$ and integrate $\cosec^2x$ using part (i).
Use $\int\cot x\,dx=\ln|\sin x|$ and evaluate at $x=\pi/2$ and $x=\pi/4$.
Keep the trigonometric values exact and convert the logarithmic term to the required form.
walkthrough:
Apply integration by parts $\int u v' = uv - \int u' v$ to $\int x\operatorname{cosec}^2 x\,\mathrm{d}x$:
Let $u = x \implies u' = 1$, and $v' = \operatorname{cosec}^2 x \implies v = -\cot x$ (from part (i)):
$$\int x\operatorname{cosec}^2 x\,\mathrm{d}x = x(-\cot x) - \int 1 \cdot (-\cot x)\,\mathrm{d}x = -x\cot x + \int \cot x\,\mathrm{d}x$$

Integrate $\cot x = \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$ using $\int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,\mathrm{d}x = \ln|f(x)|$:
$$\int \cot x\,\mathrm{d}x = \ln(\sin x)$$

Write out the full definite integral expression:
$$\left[-x\cot x + \ln(\sin x)\right]_{\frac{1}{4}\pi}^{\frac{1}{2}\pi}$$

Evaluate at the upper limit $x = \dfrac{1}{2}\pi$:
$$\cot\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\pi\right) = 0, \quad \sin\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\pi\right) = 1$$
$$\text{At } x = \dfrac{1}{2}\pi: \quad -\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\pi\right)(0) + \ln(1) = 0 + 0 = 0$$

Evaluate at the lower limit $x = \dfrac{1}{4}\pi$:
$$\cot\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\pi\right) = 1, \quad \sin\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\pi\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$$
$$\text{At } x = \dfrac{1}{4}\pi: \quad -\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\pi\right)(1) + \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{4}\pi - \ln(\sqrt{2}) = -\dfrac{1}{4}\pi - \dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2$$

Subtract the lower limit value from the upper limit value:
$$\text{Integral} = 0 - \left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\pi - \dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2\right) = \dfrac{1}{4}\pi + \dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2$$

Rewrite $\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2$ in terms of $\ln 4$ using $\ln 4 = \ln(2^2) = 2\ln 2 \implies \dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2 = \dfrac{1}{4}\ln 4$:
$$\text{Integral} = \dfrac{1}{4}\pi + \dfrac{1}{4}\ln 4 = \dfrac{1}{4}(\pi + \ln 4)$$
This completes the proof.
